summary.oneLiner: A merchant-light, PPA-heavy thermal IPP compounding EBITDA through a funded 23.7 GW thermal build-out to FY32, with optionality in hydro/nuclear and a credible path to ~INR50,000 cr EBITDA and potential debt-free status by FY31–32.
summary.business: Adani Power Limited (APL), headquartered in Ahmedabad, generates electricity primarily through coal-based thermal power plants and a solar facility spread across eight Indian states, and exports power to Bangladesh under a long-term Power Purchase Agreement signed with the Bangladesh Power Development Board in 2017. Its business model combines long-term PPAs with selectively positioned open capacity, and it predominantly caters to business-to-business (B2B) clients such as state government utilities and distribution companies (DISCOMs).

currentContext.strengths: India's largest private thermal power portfolio (18,150 MW) spread across eight states, providing economies of scale and flexibility to serve diverse demand centres|In-house coal sourcing and end-to-end logistics management, providing greater control over input costs and fuel supply reliability|High plant availability (89% O&M availability disclosed; management states availability maintained above 90% over several years) supported by digital and AI-enabled monitoring|96% of capacity contracted under long-term/medium-term PPAs, providing revenue visibility|Demonstrated track record of acquiring and turning around stressed/distressed power assets, converting more than 7 GW of capacity into profitable, cash-generating assets|Multiple credit rating upgrades since 2018 (AA/Stable from CRISIL, ICRA, India Ratings and CARE, an eight-notch upgrade since 2020), reflecting a strengthened balance sheet|High execution readiness for expansion, with 100% land secured and equipment ordering completed for the entire growth pipeline, and a brownfield-weighted mix enabling faster commissioning
currentContext.strategies: Accelerating capacity expansion toward a targeted 41,870 MW by FY 2031-32 (from an existing 18,150 MW), executed with a higher share of brownfield projects to enable faster commissioning and better capital efficiency.|Funding the majority of the expansion capex programme through internal accruals / fund flows from operations, reducing dependence on external financing and removing financial closure risk.|Embedding intelligence across operations at scale — a centralised Energy Network Operation Center (ENOC) for real-time monitoring, AI/ML-driven predictive maintenance and anomaly detection, an Analytical Center of Excellence, and a fuel tracker for coal sourcing/logistics optimisation — to strengthen control and sustain performance as the portfolio grows.|Securing long-term revenue visibility ahead of capacity build-out through long-term PPAs backed by domestic fuel linkages and availability-based tariffs.|Continuing to pursue acquisition and turnaround of stressed/distressed power assets to consolidate scale and market leadership.|Strengthening diversity and inclusion (targeted increase in female representation, the 'Unnati' leadership-building initiative) and maintaining a zero-tolerance approach to POSH.|Scaling community development through project-linked initiatives embedded within new capacity additions as more projects move into execution.|Governance materials frame Financial Capital management as 'maximise shareholders' value through sustainable growth', with stated key aspects of balanced and diversified growth, financial stability, operational excellence, and sustainable outcomes and dividend -- i.e. a philosophy of funding growth while preserving balance-sheet discipline rather than a specific payout ratio. The only dividend action disclosed in this bundle is a fixed contractual dividend on Compulsorily Redeemable Preference Shares (CCPS), paid annually on or before March 31 in terms of the contract with those preference shareholders, rather than a common-equity dividend policy.
currentContext.expansion: APL is undertaking a major brownfield-and-greenfield expansion of its own and its subsidiaries' thermal power generation capacity, developing 13 projects with a combined capacity of 23,720 MW, planned for completion by FY 2031-32, taking total combined capacity from 18,150 MW to 41,870 MW. The programme comprises 28 units of 800 MW capacity using Ultra-supercritical technology and 2 units of 660 MW capacity using Supercritical technology; of this, 14,120 MW is coming up at brownfield sites and 9,600 MW at greenfield sites. The Company states it possesses 100% of the land required and has placed advance orders with key equipment suppliers for boilers, turbines and generators across the entire programme, and has tied up 13,320 MW of the upcoming capacity under long-term Power Supply Agreements (PSAs) with state DISCOMs. New long-term PSAs signed during FY26 include: Assam Power Distribution Company Limited (APDCL) for the entire 3,200 MW (4x800 MW) greenfield Ultra-Supercritical plant to be built in Assam (Chapar) on a Design-Build-Finance-Own-Operate (DBFOO) basis using SHAKTI-linked coal; Bihar State Power Generation Company Limited (BSPGCL), on behalf of North and South Bihar DISCOMs, for a 2,400 MW (3x800 MW) greenfield USCTPP at Pirpainti, Bihar, also on DBFOO/SHAKTI terms; and Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL) for 1,500 MW (net) of power over 25 years from a 1,600 MW greenfield USCTPP at Mirzapur, UP, on a DBFOO basis. At the individual-plant level, Raipur TPP's Phase II expansion (two 800 MW ultra-supercritical units) is at an advanced stage with 54% progress and main plant equipment ordering initiated; Raigarh TPP's Phase II expansion (two 800 MW ultra-supercritical units) is 38% complete, a Phase III expansion (2x800 MW) received its Terms of Reference on 6 December 2025, and a dedicated railway line for the site is targeted for completion by June 2026. Separately, the Company completed the acquisition of Vidarbha Industries Power Limited (VIPL) during FY26 -- a 2x300 MW (600 MW) thermal plant at Butibori, Nagpur, Maharashtra -- through the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the IBC, following NCLT (Mumbai) approval of the resolution plan; the Company has also expressed interest in acting as an 'Implementing Entity' for acquiring certain power assets of Jaiprakash Associates Limited (JAL), subject to necessary approvals, as part of a resolution plan submitted by group entity Adani Enterprises Limited under JAL's ongoing CIRP.
currentContext.mdna: Rising India power demand driven by industrialisation, urban expansion and rising energy intensity, with structural demand emerging from electric mobility, data centres and manufacturing-led growth.|Renewable energy's variable nature is increasing the need for dependable, flexible thermal generation to balance supply and maintain grid stability, even as renewables continue to scale rapidly.|Coal is expected to remain the backbone of India's baseload power despite the renewable push, with thermal plants increasingly transitioning to flexible operation to manage peak demand.|India's total installed capacity is projected to reach 900 GW by 2032, with power demand growing at a 4-6% CAGR and peak demand at a faster 6-8% CAGR through FY2029-30/2032, driven by rising appliance usage, EV adoption and AI-focused data-centre load growth.|Industry-leading EBITDA margins of around 38% in the thermal segment reflect the Company's ability to convert operating scale into sustained performance.|Management describes a 'secured expansion pipeline' with 'long-term offtake visibility' underpinning near-term growth.|Land availability has been secured and ordering of critical equipment (boiler, turbine and generator packages) completed for the entire expansion pipeline.

risks.risk: Structural dependence on coal-based thermal generation amid India's energy transition
risks.note: The Company must navigate regulatory, environmental and market challenges inherent to coal-based thermal power generation in India, including the sector-wide transition toward cleaner energy, which management explicitly names as a strengthened focus area for its Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) processes in FY 2025-26.

risks.risk: Geopolitical uncertainty affecting fuel supply chains
risks.note: Management states it strengthened ERM processes in FY 2025-26 specifically to address geopolitical uncertainties affecting fuel supply chains, indicating this is viewed as a material and evolving risk to the Company's coal-dependent generation model.

Executives are described as overseeing 'operational vulnerabilities such as fuel cost changes' as part of the Company's risk culture, reflecting the direct sensitivity of thermal generation economics to coal price movements.

Equipment performance is separately flagged (alongside fuel cost and safety metrics) as an operational vulnerability actively monitored by station leadership, underscoring the criticality of plant availability and reliability to a capital-intensive thermal generation business.

The Company's ERM framework explicitly classifies risks as strategic, tactical and operational, with potential financial, operational, safety, legal, reputational or strategic impact, and requires ongoing Board-level oversight via the Risk Management Committee and four dedicated sub-committees (M&A Risk, Legal/Regulatory & Tax Risk, Reputation Risk, and Commodity Price Risk), indicating the Company itself treats its risk exposure as broad and multi-dimensional rather than confined to a single category.

one-line thesis: A merchant-light, PPA-heavy thermal IPP compounding EBITDA through a funded 23.7 GW thermal build-out to FY32, with optionality in hydro/nuclear and a credible path to ~INR50,000 cr EBITDA and potential debt-free status by FY31–32.
financial scorecard: Operational: Q4 PLF 74% (annual 66.5%); plant availability 91% (vs ~88% YoY); Q4 sales 27.2 BU; FY26 sales 99.1 BU (+3.4%); FY26 generation milestone 105 BU. PLF slightly down YoY on weak merchant prices.
guidance (verify next quarter): FY27 capacity add: 1.32 GW (Korba Phase-II) — Unit 1 commissioning Q2 FY27 (Jun–Sep), Unit 2 before year-end. VERIFY next quarter.
FY28 add: ~1.6 GW (Mahan Phase-II) — first unit targeted end-FY27, slips to Q1 FY28 if geopolitical labour/LPG constraints persist.
Korba FY27 EBITDA contribution ~INR1,000 cr (partial year), higher in FY28 (full year + PPA).
Capex: FY27 ~INR25,000 cr; FY28 ~INR33,000 cr. Total expansion program ~INR2 lakh cr.
FY27 PLF expected "far better" than Q1 FY26; demand recovery visible from Mar.
INR50,000 cr EBITDA target by FY31 (possibly FY30).
order book & pipeline: 95% of 18.15 GW operating capacity tied under long/medium-term PPA; merchant down to 5% (from 16% at start of FY26).
13.3 GW long-term PPAs tied for the 23.7 GW expansion (10.4 GW tied during FY26).

New: 1,600 MW LoA from Maharashtra DISCOM (MSEDCL); PPA not yet signed, expects sign in ~3 months then 48-month build → commissioning in 4–5 yrs; likely allocated to Raigarh / Raipur / Korba. Tariff INR5.30/unit (INR4.11 capacity + INR1.19 energy).
Market pipeline: ~13.8 GW PPA bids out (UP, Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, West Bengal, Gujarat); Gujarat issued additional 4,000 MW bid doc.
segment / subsidiary: Moxie Power (ex-Coastal Energen, full-year consolidation in FY26): drove minority-interest jump (Q3 INR8.5 cr → Q4 INR254 cr) after 558 MW medium-term PPA with Tamil Nadu for Unit 2.
Vidarbha: 600 MW operating capacity acquired during FY26, added to fixed assets (explains 25% net-fixed-asset jump vs ~6–7% capacity growth, rest is CWIP).
MSEDCL 2.5 GW RE-RTC: group product — thermal (APL) + renewable & batteries (AGEL) + PSP, served via a to-be-created group trading platform; only residual ~1–1.5% APL coal capacity feeds in.
JAL/JPVL resolution: APL as implementing agency takes 180 MW asset + JAL's 24% stake in JPVL; JPVL stations Nigrie, Bina, Vishnuprayag.
growth verticals / optionality: Hydro: 570 MW Bhutan hydro SPV incorporated; evaluating thermal/hydro/transmission beyond India.
Nuclear: several Indian SPVs incorporated; awaiting GoI rules (SMR clarity); identifying NEW (non-thermal) sites. National target 9 GW → 100 GW framed as large opportunity.
Group trading platform for bundled RTC products.
margins & cost dynamics: Fuel cost is pass-through under PPAs; states secure fuel allocation for winning bidders (de-risks fuel availability).
Imported-coal PPA tariffs lower YoY on lower import coal prices (revenue optically softer but pass-through protects margin).
New PPAs carry "materially better capacity charges" → improving return metrics; availability-based fixed charges give stable per-MW EBITDA.
No domestic coal shortage; only shipping/bunker cost uptick on imports (passed through).
capex / expansion: Goal: 23.7 GW thermal add by 2032 → ~42 GW total. Mahan Phase-II 86% complete; Raipur Phase-II 54%; Raigarh Phase-II 47%; Korba Phase-II near completion.
Korba total spend ~INR8,000–8,500 cr (incl. ~INR4,100 cr acquisition + ~INR4,000 cr new units).

Trajectory revised down near-term: FY27 cut to 1.32 GW (was 2.9 GW), FY28 to 1.6 GW (was 2.4 GW) — mgmt frames as ~6-month average deferral spilling across FY-boundaries; reaffirms 34 GW by FY30 and 4+ GW/yr commissioning FY29–FY32.
capital allocation: Conservative; majority of expansion funded by internal accruals over time, interim bridge via NCDs/corporate debt.
~INR20,000 cr annualized FFO; FY26 operational cash flow ~INR21,000 cr.
Could repay entire debt by FY31–32 → potential debt-free; large surplus thereafter to be redeployed (thermal now, nuclear/hydro/overseas later). No dividend/buyback discussed.
risks & watch-items: Merchant-price compression as RE capacity scales (mgmt's explicit thesis for de-risking via PPAs).
Execution/commissioning slippage from geopolitical labour & LPG/critical-resource availability (already pushed Mahan).
Bangladesh (BPDB) receivables: outstanding down, regular payments resuming; disputed amount with appointed expert, could escalate to Singapore arbitration (SIAC).
Rising leverage (net debt INR45,022 cr) during build phase.
Demand sensitivity to weather (early/extended monsoon depressed FY26 demand to +0.8%).
management quality / tone: Confident and execution-focused; transparent on the downward near-term capacity revision (framing as deferral, not cut) and on Mahan delay drivers. Repeatedly anchors to FY31–32 targets and conservative funding posture. Candid that PPA-vs-merchant realization is not forecastable.
non-obvious takeaways: The 27% reported EBITDA jump is partly acquisition-driven (Moxie/Vidarbha); continuing EBITDA only +9% — watch the "reported vs continuing" gap.
Merchant capacity collapse to 5% caps upside in high-price quarters but materially de-risks the RE-driven price decline mgmt expects.
MSEDCL 2.5 GW RE-RTC routes most economics to AGEL (renewables + batteries), not APL — APL contribution is marginal residual coal.
Nuclear/Bhutan-hydro are early optionality, not near-term earnings; nuclear gated entirely on pending GoI SMR rules.
qoq change log: Merchant capacity 16% (start FY26) → ~5% now; further declines as Vidarbha/Karnataka/Coastal tie-ups land.
New 1,600 MW MSEDCL LoA secured this quarter (total expansion tie-up 11.7 → 13.3 GW).
Minority interest jumped Q3 INR8.5 cr → Q4 INR254 cr on TN 558 MW medium-term PPA for Moxie Unit 2 + full-year Coastal consolidation.
FY27/FY28 capacity-add guidance revised DOWN vs last quarter (FY27 2.9→1.32 GW; FY28 2.4→1.6 GW); Mahan slipped from Dec target toward Q1 FY28.
INR7,500 cr secured NCDs raised; net debt up on capex bridge financing.
Bhutan 570 MW hydro SPV and multiple nuclear SPVs newly incorporated.

NTPC/JSWENERGY/TATAPOWER/TORNTPOWER/ADANIPOWER add thermal + RE; NHPC/SJVN/NLCINDIA on hydro/lignite; TRITURBINE/TDPOWERSYS/GVPIL on turbines/generators & aftermarket; POWERMECH on EPC + O&M.
